The prayer to God, with thanksgiving for the favour granted to him, was offered by David after the return of his anointed son Solomon to the royal palace; so that it ought strictly to have been mentioned after 1Ki 1:40. The worship of grey-headed David upon the bed recalls to mind the worship of the patriarch Jacob after making known his last will (<reference osisRef="Gen.47.31">Gen 47:31</reference>).
entries.0df057153f8ed995fbb99af2f86e4dac0c5c414a: 1Ki 1:49-50 <div eID="gen4730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4731" type="x-p"/> The news spread terror. All the guests of Adonijah fled, every man his way. Adonijah himself sought refuge from Solomon at the horns of the altar. The altar was regarded from time immemorial and among all nations as a place of refuge for criminals deserving of death; but, according to <reference osisRef="Exod.21.14">Exo 21:14</reference>, in Israel it was only allowed to afford protection in cases of unintentional slaying, and for these special cities of refuge were afterwards provided (Num 35). In the horns of the altar, as symbols of power and strength, there was concentrated the true significance of the altar as a divine place, from which there emanated both life and health (see at <reference osisRef="Exod.27.19">Exo 27:19</reference>). By grasping the horns of the altar the culprit placed himself under the protection of the saving and helping grace of God, which wipes away sin, and thereby abolishes punishment (see Bähr, <hi type="italic">Symbolik des Mos. Cult</hi>. i. p. 474). The question to what altar Adonijah fled, whether to the altar at the ark of the covenant in Zion, or to the one at the tabernacle at Gibeon, or to the one built by David on the threshing-floor of Araunah, cannot be determined with certainty. It was probably to the first of these, however, as nothing is said about a flight to Gibeon, and with regard to the altar of Araunah it is not certain that it was provided with horns like the altars of the two sanctuaries.
entries.efa27239f17aeda5adb25cd88241bfb686f78b3a: 1Ki 1:51-52 <div eID="gen4731" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4732" type="x-p"/> When this was reported to Solomon, together with the prayer of Adonijah that the king would swear to him that he would not put him to death with the sword (אם before ימית, a particle used in an oath), he promised him conditional impunity: “If he shall be brave (בּן־חיל, <hi type="italic">vir probus</hi>), none of his hair shall fall to the earth,” equivalent to not a hair of his head shall be injured (cf. <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.45">1Sa 14:45</reference>); “but if evil be found in him,” i.e., if he render himself guilty of a fresh crime, “he shall die.”
entries.4ddd3191e22f8d31f4631f9400ce213fd13a58a8: 1Ki 1:53 <div eID="gen4732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4733" type="x-p"/> He then had him fetched down from the altar (הוריד( ratl, inasmuch as the altar stood upon an eminence); and when he fell down before the king, i.e., did homage to him as king, he gave him his life and freedom in the words, “Go to thy house.” The expression לביתך לך does not imply his banishment from the court (compare 1Ki 2:13 and <reference osisRef="2Sam.14.24">2Sa 14:24</reference>). Solomon did not wish to commence his own ascent of the throne by infliction of punishment, and therefore presented the usurper with his life on the condition that he kept himself quiet.  <chapter eID="1Kgs.1"/> <div eID="gen4733" type="x-p"/>

                  <ns0:p>NOW king David was old, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi>

See <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 17. 22. Besides, this might be from the nature of his Disease, or Bo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dily Distemper.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

First, Otherwise this had been a wicked counsel and course; which therefore nei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther his Servants durst have prescribed, nor would <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> have used, especially being now in a dying condition. And seeing this was easily prevented by his taking her for his Concubine, which then was esteemed allowable, it is absurd to think that he would not chuse the safer way. 2dly, That passage <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 4. <ns0:hi>but the king knew her not,</ns0:hi> implies that the King might have had carnal knowledge of her without sin or scandal.                   <ns0:p n="36">36 And Benaiah the son of Jehoiada answered the king, and said, Amen <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Which was both an approbation of the Kings Fact, and a profession of his Allegiance to the new King, and a Petition to God to ratify and confirm it.</ns0:note>: The LORD God of my lord the king say so <ns0:hi>too</ns0:hi>

                  <ns0:p n="37">37 As the LORD hath been with my lord the king, even so be he with Solomon, and make his throne greater than the throne of my lord king David <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Which Petition, albeit it might have offended an un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />worthy, vain-glorious and envious Father, he knew would be welcome to so pious and generous a Man as <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> was, and to one so kind and indulgent to his Children.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="38">38 So Zadok the priest, and Nathan the pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phet, and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and the Che<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rethites, and the Pelethites went down, and caused Solomon to ride upon king Davids mule, and brought him to Gihon.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="39">39 And Zadok the priest <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">For though he was not the High-Priest, he might do this office, especially having the direction of the Prophet <ns0:hi>Nathan, v.</ns0:hi> 34.</ns0:note> took an horn of <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Exod. 3<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>. 25, 32.</ns0:note> oil out of the tabernacle <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">That which <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> had erected for the Ark, 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 6. 17. in which Oyl was kept for divers Sacred uses: for <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> his Tabernacle was at <ns0:hi>Gibeon,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 16. 39. and 21. 29. which was too remote for the present oc<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />casion, which required all possible expedition.</ns0:note>, and anointed Solomon: and they blew the trumpet, and all the people said, God save king Solomon.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="40">40 And all the people came up after him <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Which flocked thither in abundance, some out of curi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />osity to see so Solemn an action; others to do their Duty; and others in expectation of some advantage by their chear<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ful attendance upon the new King.</ns0:note>, and the people piped with <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> flu<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>es</ns0:note> pipes, and rejoyced with great joy <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Partly, because this would certainly prevent Civil Wars, under which they had so lately and so sorely groaned, and which they had rea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />son to fear from <ns0:hi>Adonijah's</ns0:hi> pretence to the Crown, and the assistance he might have from the great and famous Lord General <ns0:hi>Ioab,</ns0:hi> and from <ns0:hi>Abiathar</ns0:hi> the High-Priest, and from others who were or might easily be engaged for him, if <ns0:hi>Da<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vid</ns0:hi> had not ended the controversie in his life-time: and partly, because of the singular wisdom and vertue for which <ns0:hi>Solomon</ns0:hi> was even then famous. See <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 2. 5, 9.</ns0:note>, so that the earth rent <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">An Hyperbolical expression: yet even solid Bodies have been oft broken and rent by great sounds.</ns0:note> with the sound of them.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="41">41 ¶ And Adonijah, and all the guests that <ns0:hi>were</ns0:hi> with him, heard <ns0:hi>it,</ns0:hi> as they had made an end of eating <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">For <ns0:hi>Nathan</ns0:hi> having given wise counsel, took all due care to expedite the execution of it, that it might not be spoiled by delays, as frequently happens.</ns0:note>: and when Joab heard the sound of the trumpet, he said, Wherefore <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> this noise of the city, being in an uproar?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="42">42 And while he yet spake, behold, Jonathan the son of Abiathar <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Who it seems was left at <ns0:hi>Ierusalem</ns0:hi> for a Spy, as he had formerly been under <ns0:hi>Absalom.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> the priest came, and Adoni<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />jah said unto him, Come in, for thou <ns0:hi>art</ns0:hi> a valiant man <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Or; <ns0:hi>a man of vertue</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>worth,</ns0:hi> as this <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> word is used, <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 12. 4. and there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore an happy man, and hast good news for thy self and us. Compare 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 18. 27.</ns0:note>, and bringest good tidings.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="43">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:272" />43 And Jonathan answered and said to Adoni<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />jah, Verily <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>but,</ns0:hi> or, <ns0:hi>nay but;</ns0:hi> i. e. The matter is not as thou expectest, but quite contrary.</ns0:note>, our lord king David hath made Solo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mon king.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="44">44 And the king hath sent with him Zadok the priest, and Nathan the prophet, and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and the Cherethites, and the Pe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lethites, and they have caused him to ride upon the kings mule.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="45">45 And Zadok the priest, and Nathan the pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phet, have anointed him king in Gihon: and they are come up from thence rejoycing, so that the city rang again: this <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> the noise that ye have heard.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="46">46 And also Solomon sitteth on the throne <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Is put into actual possession of the Kingdom.</ns0:note> of the kingdom.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="47">47 And moreover, the kings servants came to bless our lord king David <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">To praise and thank him for his great and good care, in leaving them in the hands of so excellent a Successor, un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />der whom they might expect Peace and all Prosperity; and to congratulate with him for Gods great Mercy to him, in giving him such a Son and Successor, and that his Eyes had now seen the actual accomplishment of Gods promise made to him concerning this thing.</ns0:note>, saying, God make the name of Solomon better than thy name, and make his throne greater than thy throne. And the king bowed himself upon the bed <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Adoring God for this great Mercy, and thereby declaring his hearty approbation and consent to this action. Compare <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 47. 31.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="48">48 And also thus said the king, Blessed <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> the LORD God of Israel, which hath given <ns0:hi>one</ns0:hi> to sit on my throne this day, mine eyes even seeing <ns0:hi>it.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="49">49 And all the guests that <ns0:hi>were</ns0:hi> with Adonijah, were afraid, and rose up, and went every man his way <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> The way to his own House, lest they should be dis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />covered and taken.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="50">50 ¶ And Adonijah feared, because of Solomon, and arose, and went, and caught hold on the horns of the altar <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Either, that which was at <ns0:hi>Gibeon,</ns0:hi> as appears from 1 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 16. 39. 2 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 1. 3. and was made with four Horns, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 38. 2. to which the Sacrifices were bound, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 118. 27. Or rather, that which <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> had lately set up in the Threshing-floor of <ns0:hi>Araunah,</ns0:hi> which doubtless was made after the same form as that at <ns0:hi>Gibeon:</ns0:hi> For, First, This was next at hand. Secondly, The Altar onely is men<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tioned here, whereas in <ns0:hi>Ioab's</ns0:hi> case there is mention of the Tabernacle and Altar both, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 2. 28, 29. which seems to be noted to distinguish the two Altars: for <ns0:hi>Adonijah</ns0:hi> being the Kings Son, he might safely go to <ns0:hi>Araunah's</ns0:hi> Altar, and the People would not be forward to seize upon him, or bring him to Justice: but <ns0:hi>Ioab</ns0:hi> truly thought it was not safe for him to venture himself there, and therefore he flieth to <ns0:hi>Gibeon,</ns0:hi> as a place more remote from <ns0:hi>Ierusalem.</ns0:hi> Hither he fled, ei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther to implore Gods Mercy; or rather, to avoid <ns0:hi>Solomon's</ns0:hi> Rage; sapposing that his Reverence to that Sacred place would not permit him to pollute it with his Brothers blood; or that the consideration of Gods Grace and Mercy, which himself needed and begged of God, in pardoning his offences, and accepting the Sacrifices which he should offer there, would engage and dispose him to shew Mercy to his offend<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing and now penitent Brother; or, that his Piety would not allow him violently to pluck him as it were out of the Arms of God, into which he had put himself. And for these or such like reasons the Altar was esteemed a kind of Sanctua<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry or place of Refuge, not onely among the <ns0:hi>Gentiles,</ns0:hi> but also among the <ns0:hi>Hebrews,</ns0:hi> though it be not called by that name, as may be gathered from <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 21. 14. 1 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 2. 28.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="51">51 And it was told Solomon, saying, Behold, Adonijah feareth king Solomon: for lo, he hath caught hold on the horns of the altar, saying, Let king Solomon swear unto me to day, that he will not slay his servant <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">He owns <ns0:hi>Solomon</ns0:hi> as his King, and himself as his Servant and Subject; and being sensible of his great guilt, and of the jealousie which Kings have of their competitors, could not be satisfied without <ns0:hi>Solomon's</ns0:hi> Oath.</ns0:note> with the sword.</ns0:p>

Act. 27. 34.</ns0:note> there shall not an hair of him fall to the earth <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Herein <ns0:hi>Solomon</ns0:hi> manifests his Clemency and Brotherly affection, and withal his prudence in sparing him, whom, being his Brother, and his eldest Bro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther too, it would have been invidious to have slain.</ns0:note>: but if wickedness shall be found in him <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Not onely if he shall be guilty of some capital crime, but of a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ny great wickedness or evil design. For as this pardon was <ns0:hi>Solomon's</ns0:hi> free act, so he might justly qualify it as he pleased.</ns0:note>, he shall die.</ns0:p>
